extracted.intended_audience: educated British/public political readers and thinkers (late-18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical/political essay (pamphlet) criticizing the French Revolution and its supporters, arguing for moderation, manners, religion, and the dangers of revolutionary zeal. Not a procedural guideline — rather a set of evaluative claims about political conduct, public sentiment, and social institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid continual talk of resistance and revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The author objects to 'this continual talk of resistance and revolution' as a habitual practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such constant rhetoric 'renders the habit of society dangerously valetudinary' — it is like 'taking periodical doses' of an extreme medicine that weakens the body (society). Repeated invocation of revolution dulls the capacity for decisive action on truly great occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve extreme remedies for extreme occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme political measures (war, revolution) should not be the default response to ordinary political issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'the extreme medicine of the constitution' as a daily practice 'relaxes and wears out' the spirit necessary for real crises. The text warns against treating revolution as an everyday prescription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer qualified/civil/legal resistance where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Many situations call only for 'a qualified or... civil and legal resistance' rather than wholesale revolution or war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politicians who insist on only extremes ('It is with them a war or a revolution, or it is nothing') often end up doing no practical resistance at all when moderate measures are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of rhetorical radicalism that becomes opportunistic
rubrics_metrics.description: High-bred republicans and extreme theorists frequently become courtiers or abandon principles for trivial interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who indulge in grand theories but never intend to act can later embrace the opposite side for advantage; hypocrisy flourishes when speculation costs nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocrisy favors magnificent but empty speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypocrisy 'delights in the most sublime speculations' because it involves no real cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnificent theory without intent to act is cheap; beware praise of lofty principles that are unaccompanied by practical, consistent conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political theory must account for human nature and sympathies
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorists obsessed with abstract 'rights of man' may 'have totally forgotten his nature' and 'stop up those that lead to the heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political schemes that 'open no new avenue to the understanding' but block the path to natural sympathies will pervert moral sentiments and social affections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not celebrate or trivialize plots, massacres, or assassinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The text condemns sermons and commentaries that treat 'plots, massacres, assassinations' as a trivial price for revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraying 'cheap, bloodless reformation' as inferior and glorifying violence is morally wrong and corrosive to public taste; such triumphalism 'must shock... the moral taste of every well-born mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious rhetoric must not profane sacred expressions to praise atrocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying sacred ejaculations (e.g., 'nunc dimittis') to celebrate revolutionary bloodshed is profaning religious sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using scriptural or religious language to justify or praise 'the most horrid, atrocious, and afflicting spectacle' corrupts both religion and public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assemblies must deliberate freely, not under coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly that votes 'with a compelled appearance of deliberation' under military or mob pressure lacks liberty and impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions taken 'under the terror of the bayonet and the lamp-post and the torch' are tainted; legitimacy requires freedom from force and the ability to debate genuinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public clubs and academies should not valorize daring or violent counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Clubs and academies that take 'daring and violent and perfidious' counsel as marks of genius deform public measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public resorts treat violence and cruelty as signs of superior genius, 'humanity and compassion are ridiculed' and planning for order is corrupted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty must not be defined at the expense of property and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary extremes equate 'perfect' liberty with insecurity of property, embracing confiscation, assassination, and massacre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that amid assassination and confiscation, claims to perfect liberty are hollow; security of property is essential to a meaningful liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies should preserve decorum and not be dominated by galleries or mobs
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly where 'the gallery is in the place of the house' and riotous audiences control proceedings is an inversion of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such assemblies 'have not even the physiognomy and aspect of a grave legislative body' — legislative bodies must maintain gravity and not perform for tumultuous crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness and manners matter; do not flatter humiliation with grotesque compliments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indecent to console or congratulate humiliated persons (e.g., a dethroned monarch) by claiming great public benefits arose from their servants' murder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new 'Parisian mode of good breeding' that treats assassination-motivated 'benefits' as topics of delicate compliment is obscene; true politeness would not employ such consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery or scorn-masked 'amnesty' deepens wounds rather than heals
rubrics_metrics.description: Administering an 'anodyne draught of oblivion... powdered with all the ingredients of scorn and contempt' forces victims to drink humiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scornful amnesty or contemptuous consolation preserves 'a galling wakefulness' and perpetuates the suffering instead of offering genuine relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: History is the durable judge of political acts
rubrics_metrics.description: History 'will not forget' crimes or the era that applauded them; acts are recorded and judged by posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers and moralists should be mindful that temporary rhetorical triumphs won't erase the lasting record of atrocity or shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain chivalrous sentiments and social manners to preserve civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The loss of 'the spirit of chivalry' — generosity to rank and sex, dignified obedience, and social sentiments — will have grave consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These manners created a 'noble equality' and softened power; their extinction risks replacing tempered social honor with barbarity and baser governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws require affections and manners as supplements to mere deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws supported only 'by their own terrors' without affections and manners cannot create love, veneration, or attachment to the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting the poetic precept 'Non satis est pulchra esse poemata, dulcia sunto' — beautiful rules must be sweetened by manners; the emotional and social fabric supplements legal precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning must be protected by social institutions, not corrupted into dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning grew under the protection of 'the nobility and the clergy' and in turn enlarged their ideas; if learning aspires to be master it becomes debauched by ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the 'indissoluble union' of learning and its natural protectors; avoid turning learning into a political master that dethrones its patrons and becomes subject to faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic prosperity (commerce/manufacture) depends on manners and supporting institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce, trade, and manufacture 'grew under the same shade in which learning flourished' and may decay if the social supports (manners, religion, patronage) are removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political experiments that destroy ancient principles risk impoverishing a nation culturally and economically — the social ecosystem (manners, religion, patrons) sustains economic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banishing affections invites more brutal methods of power retention
rubrics_metrics.description: If manners and ancient principles are removed, rulers will hold power by 'preventive murder and preventive confiscation' and grim maxims of brutal governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that usurpation that destroys the principles that once restrained power will resort to anticipatory, violent measures to maintain control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Europe has a shared stake in the preservation of manners and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because nations influence each other's manners, the 'fountain' of manners in France, if 'choked up and polluted', threatens to contaminate the stream to England and the rest of Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author frames French developments as a continental concern — observers should consider cross-national cultural influence when evaluating revolutionary changes.
